rawGaps.recommendation: Add a named OSHA citation in the 'Popliteal Pressure Problem' or 'How Seat Depth Relates to Thigh Length' section. Specifically reference 'OSHA eTools: Computer Workstations – Chairs' with a direct link to osha.gov/etools/computer-workstations/components/chairs. One sentence is sufficient: 'OSHA's Computer Workstations guide independently corroborates this threshold, noting that a seat too deep creates pressure behind the knees while a seat too shallow fails to support the thighs.' This closes the authoritative-source gap that eurekaergonomic.com exploits and strengthens the page's E-E-A-T signal for the primary benchmark query.

rawGaps.gap: No mmHg or pressure-mapping data quantifying popliteal compression risk — competitor cites a biomechanical pressure range of 60–100 mmHg as a threshold for impaired venous/arterial flow; TCA describes the mechanism qualitatively but provides no numeric pressure figures
rawGaps.recommendation: In the 'Popliteal Pressure Problem' section, add one sentence anchoring the risk to a numeric pressure threshold, e.g.: 'Biomechanical pressure mapping research estimates popliteal compression from an ill-fitted seat edge can reach 60–100 mmHg — a range associated with impaired venous return in soft tissue.' Attribute it honestly (cite the same soft-tissue compression literature TCA already references via PubMed) and include a brief caveat that individual sensitivity varies. This adds measurement specificity to the mechanism section without fabricating clinical claims.

rawGaps.gap: Seat depth criteria checklist from Cornell's chair-selection guidance is not surfaced — the Cornell 'How to Choose an Ergonomic Chair' page lists seat pan fit as a discrete pass/fail criterion ('seat pan should not be too long… otherwise it will catch you behind the knees'); TCA explains the rule but never formats it as a scannable pass/fail checklist a user can apply while evaluating a specific chair
rawGaps.recommendation: Add a 3–4 item 'Chair Seat Depth Checklist' callout box inside or immediately after the 'Adjustable Seat Depth vs Fixed Seat Depth' section, framed as a Cornell-sourced evaluation tool. Items: (1) Seat pan depth meets your measured minimum requirement; (2) 2–3 finger clearance achievable when sitting fully back; (3) Seat slider present if your requirement exceeds the chair's fixed depth; (4) Seat pan does not force you to sit forward to relieve knee pressure. This converts the explanatory prose TCA already has into an actionable decision aid and mirrors the checklist format Cornell uses on its own guidance page.

rawGaps.gap: The FAQ does not include a question addressing what happens when a seat is TOO DEEP (overhang in the other direction) — both Cornell and Eureka explicitly note that excess depth forces posterior pelvic tilt and loss of lumbar contact, but TCA's FAQ only covers the too-shallow scenario
rawGaps.recommendation: Add one FAQ entry: 'Can a seat be too deep for tall users?' Answer should clarify that while tall users most commonly need more depth, a seat that exceeds thigh length by more than 3 finger-widths forces the user to sit forward, losing lumbar support contact — the same compensatory posture cascade described in the body content. Note that the Leap Plus's 4-inch slider range means a tall user set at maximum depth who has shorter-than-expected thighs can retract the slider. Keep the answer under 100 words. This covers a genuine sub-question that appears in competitor content and prevents the page from appearing one-sided on the measurement question.
